title: Record ownership
summary: Restrict repository access with the identity already established by Spring Security.

richText: Spring Security checks authorities. It does not infer ownership from a JPA entity.
can allow two users to call the same endpoint.
The service still needs to restrict each user to records that account owns.
Spring provides the trusted identity through the authenticated principal.
A request path or body cannot establish who the current user is.
A repository query can include both the requested record ID and the authenticated owner ID.
This returns a record only when both values match.
Read, update, and delete operations all need the same ownership boundary.
The service checks ownership before changing a record.
A missing record and a record owned by another user can both return
An immutable account ID is a better ownership key when usernames can change.

example.title: Restrict JPA employees to their creating account
description: Each example is a separate project. All required application files appear in the tabs.
The example uses an in-memory H2 database. Restarting the application clears its records.
The generated form login authenticates the `reader` account.
After login, `GET /csrf` returns the session CSRF token. A state-changing request sends that token under the returned header name with the session cookie.
The account creating an employee owns that record.
Usernames cannot change in this example. A system with renameable usernames needs an immutable account ID instead.
`EmployeeController` calls the injected `OwnedEmployeeService` through its Spring proxy.
For an existing production database, the ownership column and real owner values require a migration before enforcing a non-null constraint.
explanation: `@PreAuthorize` rejects an anonymous caller before either service operation runs.
`create` obtains the owner from Spring Security rather than accepting it in the request.
The additional constructor stores that owner with the new employee.
`updatable = false` excludes the owner column from ordinary JPA updates.
Spring Data derives a query that matches both `id` and `ownerUsername`.
No matching record produces `404`, including when another user owns the ID.
Update and delete paths need the same owner-scoped lookup before changing a record.
The password username used here is not automatically the same identity as a JWT subject. A JWT application needs an explicit local-account mapping.
